influences/easter-name-and-eostre/name: Easter: Passover roots, the name Eostre and the Ishtar myth
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/source: The Jewish Passover (Pesach). The Anglo-Saxon month Eosturmonath, said by Bede to be named after a goddess Eostre
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/christ: Pascha, the annual feast of Christ's death and resurrection, called 'Easter' only in English and 'Ostern' in German
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/eviden: The feast itself comes from the Jewish Passover. Most languages call it by derivatives of Pascha, from Hebrew pesach (Pâques, Pascua, Pasqua, Paskha). The claim that it derives from Ishtar has no evidence at all. Only the English and German name has a possible pagan link. Bede (De temporum ratione 15, 725) says Eosturmonath was named after a goddess Eostre. Some scholars doubt she existed. Philip Shaw argues plausibly for a local deity, but the name is the only thing at stake.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/popula: Easter is a pagan fertility festival of the goddess Ishtar or Eostre, with eggs and rabbits as fertility symbols. 'Easter' is pronounced like 'Ishtar', and Christians simply renamed it.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/whatHi: Christians celebrated Pascha as a Christian Passover from at least the second century. The Quartodecimans of Asia Minor kept it on 14 Nisan, and Melito of Sardis' Peri Pascha (c.165) is a Christian Passover homily. Rome kept the following Sunday. Disputes over the date involved Polycarp and Anicetus (c.155), Victor and Irenaeus (c.190), Nicaea (325) and the Synod of Whitby (664). All of them presuppose a Jewish, not a pagan, starting point. The English word appears only because Anglo-Saxon converts kept their month name for April. Bede is the sole source for Eostre. Jacob Grimm (1835) expanded her into a Germanic goddess 'Ostara', and later writers attached hares and eggs to her without ancient evidence. 'Ishtar' is a Mesopotamian goddess with no historical or linguistic connection to the English word. The link was popularised by Alexander Hislop's The Two Babylons (1853) and by a widely shared internet meme in 2013. Easter eggs go back to the Lenten ban on eating eggs, and the Easter hare is first recorded in seventeenth-century Germany.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/summar: Easter is the Christian Passover. Its date, theology and name in most languages (Pascha) come from Judaism. Only the English name may echo a pagan goddess, Eostre, known from a single sentence of Bede. The popular claim that Easter derives from Ishtar is a modern myth.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/story:
Jesus was crucified at Passover, and the earliest Christians read his death through the Passover lamb: 'Christ our Passover is sacrificed for us' (1 Corinthians 5:7). The annual feast that grew from this was called Pascha, the Greek and Aramaic form of pesach. In the second century the churches of Asia Minor, claiming the authority of John and Polycarp, kept it on 14 Nisan whatever the day of the week. Rome and most other churches kept it on the following Sunday. Polycarp and Anicetus agreed to differ in Rome c.155. Pope Victor's threat to excommunicate the Asians c.190 drew a rebuke from Irenaeus (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.23–25).

The Council of Nicaea (325) settled on a common Sunday celebration calculated by the church rather than by contemporary Jewish reckoning. Constantine's letter after the council shows hostility to dependence on the Jews. Later disputes were about calculation tables, not paganism. The best-known was the clash between Irish and Roman reckonings settled at the Synod of Whitby in 664 (Bede, Ecclesiastical History 3.25). Melito of Sardis' Peri Pascha (c.165), the Apostolic Tradition and the fourth-century Jerusalem rites described by Egeria all show a feast built on Exodus typology, baptism and the Gospel Passion narratives.

The English name is the exception. In The Reckoning of Time (725), Bede explains the old English month names: 'Eosturmonath, which is now interpreted as the paschal month, was once named after a goddess of theirs called Eostre, in whose honour feasts were celebrated in that month'. No other source mentions her. Some scholars think Bede guessed from the month name. Philip Shaw links her to the Germanic root for 'east' and 'dawn' and to the Matronae Austriahenae of Roman Rhineland inscriptions. Old High German Ostarun gave modern German Ostern. Nearly every other Christian language, including Welsh (Pasg), Dutch (Pasen) and Scandinavian (påske), uses Pascha.

The pagan-origins story was elaborated much later. Jacob Grimm's Deutsche Mythologie (1835) reconstructed a goddess Ostara. Alexander Hislop's anti-Catholic The Two Babylons (1853) equated Easter with Astarte and Ishtar, and this was later repeated in Jehovah's Witness and Armstrong literature and in a viral image of 2013. Easter eggs have a Christian history. Eggs were forbidden during the Lenten fast, so they were saved, decorated and blessed for Easter. Mesopotamian Christians dyed them red for Christ's blood. The Easter hare is first described by Georg Franck von Franckenau in De ovis paschalibus (1682). Folklorists now generally treat the hare-and-egg 'fertility goddess' explanation as a nineteenth-century invention rather than an ancient survival.

Some traditions avoid Easter because of its name or its customs. These include some Restorationist and Hebrew Roots groups, Jehovah's Witnesses (who keep only an annual Memorial on 14 Nisan) and the Worldwide Church of God under Herbert W. Armstrong. Under later leadership that church, renamed Grace Communion International, adopted Easter in the 1990s. Most churches, Eastern and Western, regard the Pascha-Passover link as the heart of the feast.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/howItH: Jesus' death at Passover led the first Christians to interpret it as the true paschal sacrifice (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 19:36).
Second-century churches kept an annual Pascha, either on 14 Nisan (Quartodecimans) or on the following Sunday.
Nicaea (325) required a common Sunday date computed by Christian tables, later standardised as the first Sunday after the paschal full moon.
Anglo-Saxon converts kept the native month name Eosturmonath for the paschal season, which gave English its word 'Easter'.
Lenten fasting made eggs a natural Easter food, and later German folklore added the Easter hare (1682).
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/exampl: Melito of Sardis, Peri Pascha (c.165): a sermon on Exodus 12 read as a prophecy of Christ.
Polycarp and Anicetus's agreement to differ on the date of Pascha, c.155 (Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.24).
Bede, De temporum ratione 15: the only source for the goddess Eostre.
The Synod of Whitby (664) adopts the Roman Easter reckoning in Northumbria.
Pascha-derived names: Greek Pascha, Latin Pascha, French Pâques, Spanish Pascua, Russian Paskha, Welsh Pasg.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/defend: Kept the Asian 14 Nisan Pascha, which he said came from John, and defended it in Rome c.155. Evidence of the feast's Jewish-Christian roots.
Urged Victor of Rome not to break communion over differing Pascha dates (c.190).
Recorded the Eostre etymology without embarrassment and wrote the standard medieval treatise on calculating Easter.
influences/easter-name-and-eostre/critic: His The Two Babylons (1853) claimed Easter was the Babylonian Astarte or Ishtar festival, an assertion without historical basis that is still widely repeated.
Reject Easter customs as pagan and keep instead an annual Memorial of Christ's death on 14 Nisan.
Herbert W. Armstrong (Worldwide Church of God)
Taught that Easter was pagan and kept the biblical Passover and feasts instead. His successors reversed this in the 1990s.

influences/latin-greek-language/name: Latin and Greek: the languages of the church
influences/latin-greek-language/sourceCu: Koine Greek and Latin, including the civic vocabulary of the polis and the formal register of Roman sacral prayer
influences/latin-greek-language/christia: The Greek New Testament and liturgy, Christian Latin, the Vulgate, the Roman Rite and a theological vocabulary in both languages
influences/latin-greek-language/evidence: That Christianity took over Greek and Latin — and with them civic, legal, philosophical and even pagan religious vocabulary — is documented in every surviving text. Christine Mohrmann showed that Roman liturgical Latin deliberately adopted the solemn style of Roman sacral prayer. The claim that Latin worship was a pagan imposition or a device to keep the Bible from the people is a polemical myth.
influences/latin-greek-language/popularC: The Latin Mass is a relic of pagan Rome, kept so that ordinary people could not understand the Bible or the liturgy.
influences/latin-greek-language/whatHist: Christianity began in Aramaic and spread in Greek: the New Testament and the Septuagint were Greek, and the church of Rome itself worshipped and wrote in Greek until the third century (Clement, Hippolytus). Latin Christianity first appears in North Africa (the Scillitan martyrs, 180; Tertullian). Rome switched to Latin liturgy in the later fourth century, probably under Pope Damasus, precisely because Latin had become the vernacular of the city; the canon of the Mass is quoted by Ambrose (De sacramentis, c. 390). Jerome’s Vulgate (382–405) was commissioned to give a reliable Latin Bible for ordinary readers. Christine Mohrmann demonstrated that the Roman prayers deliberately used the archaic, solemn, legalistic style of pagan Roman prayer to sound dignified. Only later, as Latin ceased to be spoken, did it become a barrier — a problem the Reformers addressed with vernacular worship and the Catholic Church with Vatican II.
influences/latin-greek-language/summary: Christianity spoke the languages of the Roman world and borrowed their vocabulary — civic, legal, philosophical and religious. Latin and Greek began as vernaculars for mission and only later became sacred languages that divided clergy from people.
influences/latin-greek-language/story:
The first Christians spoke Aramaic, but within a generation the movement’s texts were written in koine Greek, the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. Greek gave the church its name — ekklesia, the citizens’ assembly of a Greek city — and words such as leitourgia (a public service paid for by a citizen), episkopos (overseer), presbyteros (elder), diakonos (servant) and mysterion. Later theology drew on the philosophical Greek of ousia, hypostasis, physis and homoousios, which became the language of the creeds at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451).

Latin Christianity began not in Rome but in North Africa. The Acts of the Scillitan Martyrs (180) are the oldest dated Latin Christian text; Tertullian (c. 200) coined or gave a Christian sense to trinitas, persona, substantia and sacramentum (originally a soldier’s oath of allegiance). The Roman church wrote in Greek until the third century — Clement and Hippolytus wrote in Greek — and changed its liturgy to Latin in the later fourth century, when Greek was no longer understood by most Roman Christians. Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome to revise the Old Latin Bible (382), and the resulting Vulgate became the standard Western Bible for a thousand years.

Christine Mohrmann’s studies of liturgical Latin showed that the Roman collects and canon deliberately imitated the archaic, solemn and legally precise register of Roman pagan prayer — doubled phrases, technical terms such as propitius, hostia, praesta quaesumus — to sound dignified in a society that associated religion with ancient formulae. At the same time Christian Latin transformed words: ‘pagan’ itself comes from paganus (a civilian or country dweller), used by Christians for non-Christians from the fourth century; gratia, salus, fides and religio acquired new meanings; Augustine’s On Christian Teaching (397–426) argued that classical rhetoric and learning could be ‘spoiled’ from the Egyptians for Christian use.

Once Latin ceased to be spoken, it became a learned and sacred language. Isidore of Seville and Bede taught it as a second language; Charlemagne’s reforms standardised it; the idea emerged of three sacred languages — Hebrew, Greek and Latin — inscribed on the Cross (John 19:20). Cyril and Methodius challenged this ‘trilingual’ view by creating Slavonic letters and liturgy, which Popes Hadrian II (868) and John VIII (880) approved. Humanists such as Lorenzo Valla and Erasmus returned to the Greek text and criticised the Vulgate, and Erasmus’s Greek New Testament (1516) underlay Luther’s German Bible.

The Reformers made vernacular worship a principle: Luther’s German Mass (1526) and Cranmer’s Book of Common Prayer (1549), whose Article 24 condemned services in ‘a tongue not understanded of the people’. The Council of Trent (1562) kept Latin while requiring that the Mass be explained in preaching. The Second Vatican Council (Sacrosanctum Concilium 36, 1963) permitted the vernacular, and Paul VI’s Missal (1969–70) was soon celebrated almost entirely in modern languages. Benedict XVI widened use of the older Latin rite (Summorum Pontificum, 2007), and Pope Francis restricted it again (Traditionis custodes, 2021). Greek remains the liturgical language of the Greek Orthodox churches, while other Orthodox and Oriental churches use Church Slavonic, Coptic, Ge’ez, Syriac and Armenian alongside modern vernaculars.
influences/latin-greek-language/howItHap: The church adopted koine Greek and its civic vocabulary (ekklesia, leitourgia, episkopos) for mission across the eastern Mediterranean.
Latin Christianity developed in North Africa, where Tertullian forged a theological vocabulary from legal and everyday Latin.
Rome moved its liturgy from Greek to Latin in the later fourth century because Latin was the vernacular.
Roman prayers adopted the solemn style of pagan Roman sacral language, and Greek philosophy supplied doctrinal terms.
As Latin ceased to be spoken it became a sacred language, challenged by Slavonic missions, humanists, the Reformers and Vatican II.

influences/latin-greek-language/defender: Argued in On Christian Teaching that pagan learning and rhetoric could be taken over like the Israelites’ ‘spoiling of the Egyptians’.
Produced the Vulgate from Hebrew and Greek, making a Latin Bible in the vernacular of his time.
Defended worship in Slavonic against the ‘trilingual’ view that only Hebrew, Greek and Latin were fit for liturgy.
Defended Latin and the older Roman rite as a treasure of the church’s tradition (Summorum Pontificum, 2007).
influences/latin-greek-language/critics/: Warned against philosophy’s influence on doctrine (‘What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?’), even as he shaped Latin theological vocabulary.
Translated the Bible and wrote the German Mass (1526) so that worship would be understood by the people.
His Book of Common Prayer (1549) replaced Latin with English, and the Articles condemned worship in an unknown tongue.
Implemented a vernacular liturgy after Vatican II while urging that Latin and chant not be lost.

influences/latin-greek-language/keptBy/3: Classical languages in Protestant and Catholic theological education
